Neonatal giant pandas are among the most altricial of all placental mammals, with newborn cubs weighing a mere 151.5 grams [Wwb = 151.5 grams] at birth, a value that represents less than one-thousandth of the mother's body mass. This extreme altriciality is thought to be an evolutionary consequence of delayed implantation and a short, energetically constrained gestation period. Under the species' core body temperature of 37.0 °C [T = 37.0 °C], the gestation time itself has been documented at 48 days [tg = 48 days], a duration that includes a highly variable period of embryonic diapause. Following parturition, the cub is entirely dependent on maternal care, and the onset of suckling occurs within hours of birth. The neonatal stage is characterized by rapid but fragile growth, with the cub's eyes remaining sealed for the first several weeks of life, a trait shared with other ursids that produce such altricial young. This extreme dependency on maternal provisioning sets the stage for an extended period of postnatal care that is among the longest of any terrestrial mammal.

The nursing period in Ailuropoda melanoleuca is remarkably prolonged compared to other ursids, a reflection of the cub's extremely small birth size and slow developmental trajectory. Under the stable thermal conditions of maternal care at 37.0 °C [T = 37.0 °C], weaning, defined as the cessation of milk dependency and the transition to a solid bamboo diet, typically occurs at 182 days since birth [tx = 182 days since birth]. At this nutritional independence milestone, the cub attains a wet weight at weaning of approximately 22000 grams [Wwx = approximately 22000 grams], representing a dramatic 145-fold increase from its birth mass. This period of rapid mass gain is fueled entirely by the mother's lipid-rich milk, which is among the highest in fat content of any terrestrial mammal. The weaning transition is gradual, with cubs beginning to consume small amounts of bamboo shoots while still occasionally nursing, a behavioral pattern that facilitates the shift to an adult diet.

By the time a giant panda cub reaches its first birthday, its body mass has increased to roughly 40000 grams , reflecting a sustained period of intense growth on an exclusively bamboo diet following weaning. This mass of 40000 grams  at one year since birth is still well below the ultimate asymptotic size the animal will achieve as a full adult. The juvenile and sub-adult stages are characterized by a gradual deceleration in growth rate as the animal approaches reproductive maturation. Under normal physiological temperatures of 37.0 °C [T = 37.0 °C], puberty, or the onset of sexual maturation, occurs at 2192 days since birth [tp = 2192 days since birth], which corresponds to approximately six years of age. This delayed maturation is typical of large-bodied, long-lived mammals with a slow life-history pace, and it is accompanied by the development of adult social behaviors and the establishment of a permanent olfactory communication system through scent marking.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult giant panda is recorded at approximately 117500 grams [Wwi = approximately 117500 grams], an asymptotic mass that is reached by around eight to ten years of age and places the species among the largest members of the family Ursidae, though it is notably smaller than its polar bear and brown bear relatives. Reproductive output in this species is exceptionally low for a mammal of its size, with females typically producing a single cub per litter [N_R_i = single cub per litter] in most reproductive events, and twinning occurring only rarely. Furthermore, females exhibit a very low reproductive frequency, limited to one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years] in the wild, which is constrained by the prolonged period of maternal investment required to wean a single offspring. This extremely low annual reproductive rate is a critical factor in the species' vulnerability to population decline.

Longevity data from both wild and captive populations indicate that the maximum lifespan for the giant panda is approximately 36.8 years [am = approximately 36.8 years] when the animal is maintained under the standard physiological temperature of 37.0 °C [T = 37.0 °C], a value consistent with that of other large ursids and reflecting a life-history strategy characterized by delayed reproduction, extended parental care, and a slow pace of life. As individuals approach the senescent stage, they often exhibit a decline in locomotor efficiency and a reduction in daily bamboo intake, leading to a gradual loss of body condition. Comparative studies across ursid species suggest that the giant panda's combination of extreme altricial birth, protracted juvenile dependency, and very low fecundity represents an endpoint along a continuum of life-history strategies that have evolved in response to the low nutritional quality of their bamboo diet and the stable, predictable environment of their montane forest habitat.
